phy-0-0.intro:
Mechanics begins with a narrower question than "why do things move": given a body moving along a straight line, how do we describe exactly where it is at every instant, how fast its position changes, and how fast that rate itself changes? This descriptive part of mechanics is called **kinematics**. It matters because every later law is stated in its language. Newton's second law says that force determines acceleration, so until acceleration is a precise quantity the law has no content.

The tool that makes the description precise is calculus. Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, acceleration is the derivative of velocity, and the reverse questions (where will the body be, given how it accelerates) are answered by integration with initial conditions. In this chapter you will build these definitions, learn to read them off graphs as slopes and areas, derive the familiar constant-acceleration equations as a special case, and apply them to free fall and to problems in which two bodies must meet.

sections.md:
This section answers the first question of kinematics: how do we attach numbers to "where" and "how far" for a body moving on a line, in a way that keeps track of direction?

**Coordinate axis and position.** Choose a straight line along which the motion happens, pick a point on it as the origin, and choose one direction as positive. The **position** of the particle is its signed coordinate \( x \) on this axis, measured in meters. Because the particle moves, position is a function of time, \( x(t) \). The choice of origin and positive direction is yours; physical conclusions never depend on it, but every sign in the solution does, so state it at the start of every problem.

**Displacement.** Between times \( t_1 \) and \( t_2 \) the **displacement** is
\[ \Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1). \]
It is signed: positive if the net change is in the positive direction. Displacement depends only on the endpoints, not on the route.

**Distance traveled.** The **distance traveled** is the total length of path covered, counting every segment as positive. If the particle reverses direction, distance exceeds \( |\Delta x| \). Distance is never negative.

**Average velocity and average speed.** Over the interval \( \Delta t = t_2 - t_1 \),
\[ v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}, \qquad \text{average speed} = \frac{\text{distance traveled}}{\Delta t}. \]
Average velocity is signed and carries the direction of the net displacement; average speed is non-negative. Since distance is at least \( |\Delta x| \), average speed is always at least \( |v_{\text{avg}}| \), with equality exactly when the particle never reverses during the interval.

Geometrically, \( v_{\text{avg}} \) is the slope of the **secant line** joining the two points \( (t_1, x(t_1)) \) and \( (t_2, x(t_2)) \) on the graph of position against time.

**Worked example.** A runner on a straight track starts at \( x = 2.0 \) m, runs to \( x = 50.0 \) m in 8.0 s, then turns and jogs back to \( x = 30.0 \) m in a further 4.0 s. Take the positive direction as the direction of the first leg.

1. Displacement: \( \Delta x = 30.0 - 2.0 = 28.0 \) m.
2. Distance: the first leg covers \( 50.0 - 2.0 = 48.0 \) m, the second \( 50.0 - 30.0 = 20.0 \) m, so the distance is \( 68.0 \) m.
3. Total time: \( \Delta t = 12.0 \) s.
4. Average velocity: \( v_{\text{avg}} = 28.0/12.0 = 2.33 \) m/s, in the positive direction.
5. Average speed: \( 68.0/12.0 = 5.67 \) m/s.

The two differ because the runner reversed direction; the 20.0 m jogged back counts toward distance but cancels part of the displacement.

**Common mistake.** Averaging the velocities of the separate legs. The runner's leg velocities are \( 48.0/8.0 = 6.0 \) m/s and \( -20.0/4.0 = -5.0 \) m/s; their arithmetic mean, \( 0.5 \) m/s, is not the average velocity. The definition divides the total displacement by the total time, which weights each leg by how long it lasted. The simple mean of velocities agrees with this only when the legs last equal times (or have equal velocities).

A second, related mistake is to treat "average velocity zero" as "the body did not move". A round trip has zero displacement and so zero average velocity, while the distance traveled and the average speed are positive.

Dividing by \( \Delta t > 0 \) gives \( |v_{\text{avg}}| \le D/\Delta t \), the average speed. Equality in the triangle inequality holds exactly when all nonzero \( d_i \) have the same sign, that is, when the particle never reverses direction during the interval. (In integral form: \( |\int v\,dt| \le \int |v|\,dt \).)

sections.title: Position, displacement, and average velocity

sections.md:
Average velocity describes a whole interval. The speedometer, however, reports a value at an instant. This section makes "velocity at an instant" precise and then does the same for the rate of change of velocity.

**Instantaneous velocity.** Shrink the interval: the average velocity over \( [t, t + \Delta t] \) is \( \big(x(t+\Delta t) - x(t)\big)/\Delta t \). The **instantaneous velocity** is its limit,
\[ v(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{x(t + \Delta t) - x(t)}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}. \]
This is exactly the derivative from calculus, so the secant slope of the previous section becomes the slope of the **tangent line** to the \( x \)-\( t \) graph. The **speed** is \( |v(t)| \), the magnitude of the velocity. Velocity is signed and says which way the particle moves; speed does not.

**Acceleration.** Applying the same construction to velocity gives the **acceleration**,
\[ a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}, \]
measured in m/s². Acceleration is the slope of the \( v \)-\( t \) graph.

**Speeding up or slowing down.** The sign of \( a \) alone does not tell you whether the particle is getting faster. Differentiate the square of the speed: \( \frac{d}{dt}(v^2) = 2v\,\frac{dv}{dt} = 2va \). So the speed increases when \( v \) and \( a \) have the same sign and decreases when they have opposite signs. A negative acceleration with a negative velocity means speeding up in the negative direction.

**Worked example.** A particle moves according to \( x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t \), with \( x \) in meters and \( t \) in seconds (the coefficients carry the units needed to make each term meters).

1. Velocity: \( v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t-1)(t-3) \) m/s.
2. Acceleration: \( a(t) = 6t - 12 \) m/s².
3. The particle is momentarily at rest when \( v = 0 \): at \( t = 1 \) s (where \( x = 4 \) m) and \( t = 3 \) s (where \( x = 0 \)). Between these times \( v < 0 \), so it moves in the negative direction.
4. At \( t = 2 \) s: \( v = -3 \) m/s and \( a = 0 \). For \( 1 < t < 2 \), \( v < 0 \) and \( a < 0 \): speeding up. For \( 2 < t < 3 \), \( v < 0 \) and \( a > 0 \): slowing down.

In the plot below the horizontal axis is time \( t \) and the vertical axis is position \( x \). Drag \( s \) to move the tangent line along the curve and watch its slope: it is positive before \( t = 1 \), zero at the peak and trough, and steepest downward at \( t = 2 \), where the velocity is most negative.

```plot
x: 0, 4
y: -2, 6
xlabel: t (s)
ylabel: x (m)
f: x^3 - 6*x^2 + 9*x | position x(t)
slider: s, 0, 4, 0.5 | instant s
f: (3*s^2 - 12*s + 9)*(x - s) + s^3 - 6*s^2 + 9*s | tangent at t = s
point: s, s^3 - 6*s^2 + 9*s
```

**Common mistake.** Reading "negative acceleration" as "deceleration". Deceleration means the speed is decreasing, which requires \( v \) and \( a \) to have opposite signs. On \( 1 < t < 2 \) above, the acceleration is negative and the particle is speeding up. The second common mistake is to conclude that \( a = 0 \) whenever \( v = 0 \); at \( t = 1 \) the particle is at rest but \( a = -6 \) m/s², which is why it does not stay at rest.

The acceleration's direction is not the direction of motion, and a positive \( a \) means speeding up only when \( v > 0 \).

sections.title: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration as derivatives

sections.md:
In practice the arrow of inference usually runs the other way. Newton's laws (next chapters) will tell you the acceleration; you then want velocity and position. This section reverses differentiation.

**Velocity from acceleration.** Since \( dv/dt = a \), the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives
\[ v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a(t')\,dt', \qquad x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t v(t')\,dt', \]
where \( v_0 = v(0) \) and \( x_0 = x(0) \) are the **initial conditions**. The dummy variable \( t' \) keeps the upper limit distinct from the integration variable. Knowing \( a(t) \) alone does not determine the motion: two particles with the same acceleration but different starting velocities follow different paths. You always need one initial condition per integration.

**Worked example.** A car starts from rest at \( x = 0 \) and for \( 0 \le t \le 6.0 \) s has \( a(t) = 3.0 - 0.50t \) (in m/s², with \( t \) in s).

1. \( v(t) = 0 + \int_0^t (3.0 - 0.50t')\,dt' = 3.0t - 0.25t^2 \) m/s.
2. \( v(6.0) = 18 - 9.0 = 9.0 \) m/s.
3. \( x(t) = \int_0^t (3.0t' - 0.25t'^2)\,dt' = 1.5t^2 - t^3/12 \) m.
4. \( x(6.0) = 54 - 18 = 36 \) m.

Note that you could not have used "distance equals average acceleration times time squared" formulas here; the acceleration changes with time.

**The graphical meaning.** The definite integral is signed area. Hence:
- the signed area under the \( a \)-\( t \) graph over an interval is the change in velocity;
- the signed area under the \( v \)-\( t \) graph is the displacement.

Area below the axis counts negatively. That is exactly right for displacement, but it means the \( v \)-\( t \) area does not give distance when the particle reverses. The distance traveled is
\[ D = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v(t)|\,dt, \]
computed in practice by finding where \( v = 0 \), splitting the interval there, and adding the absolute values of the pieces.

**Worked example (distance versus displacement).** Let \( v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3 = (t-1)(t-3) \) m/s on \( 0 \le t \le 4 \) s. The signed area is
\[ \int_0^4 (t^2 - 4t + 3)\,dt = \Big[\tfrac{t^3}{3} - 2t^2 + 3t\Big]_0^4 = \tfrac{4}{3} \text{ m}. \]
Splitting at the zeros: \( \int_0^1 v\,dt = \tfrac43 \), \( \int_1^3 v\,dt = -\tfrac43 \), \( \int_3^4 v\,dt = \tfrac43 \). So the displacement is \( \tfrac43 \) m but the distance is \( \tfrac43 + \tfrac43 + \tfrac43 = 4 \) m.

In the plot the horizontal axis is \( t \) and the vertical axis is \( v \). The shaded region between 1 and 3 lies below the axis; in the displacement it cancels one of the two positive lobes, while the distance counts all three lobes.

```plot
x: 0, 4.2
y: -1.5, 3.5
xlabel: t (s)
ylabel: v (m/s)
f: x^2 - 4*x + 3 | v(t)
shade: x^2 - 4*x + 3, 0, 4 | signed area = displacement
```

**Common mistake.** Forgetting the constant. Writing \( v = \int a\,dt = 3.0t - 0.25t^2 \) is right above only because the car started from rest. If it had started at 5.0 m/s, every later velocity would be 5.0 m/s larger, and every position would change by \( 5.0t \). An indefinite integral is a family of functions; the initial condition picks the member that describes this particle.

questions.prompt: A particle has acceleration \( a(t) = (6.0\ \text{m/s}^3)\,t \), with \( v(0) = -3.0 \) m/s and \( x(0) = 2.0 \) m. Find its position at \( t = 2.0 \) s, in meters.
For the particle in the previous question, find the total distance it travels between \( t = 0 \) and \( t = 2.0 \) s, in meters.
questions.why: \( v = 3t^2 - 3 \) vanishes at \( t = 1 \) s. Positions: \( x(0) = 2 \), \( x(1) = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0 \), \( x(2) = 4 \). The particle moves 2 m in the negative direction, then 4 m in the positive direction: distance \( 6.0 \) m, although the displacement is only \( +2.0 \) m.

sections.title: Recovering motion from acceleration: integrals and areas

sections.md:
Many situations (a car braking steadily, a body falling near Earth's surface without air resistance) have an acceleration that is constant to good accuracy. In that case the integrals of the previous section can be done once and for all, giving a small set of equations that relate \( x \), \( v \), \( a \) and \( t \). This section derives them, so that you know exactly when they hold.

**Derivation.** Let \( a \) be constant, with \( x(0) = x_0 \) and \( v(0) = v_0 \).

1. Integrate the acceleration: \( v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t a\,dt' \), so
\[ v = v_0 + at. \qquad (1) \]
2. Integrate the velocity: \( x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t (v_0 + at')\,dt' \), so
\[ x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac12 a t^2. \qquad (2) \]
3. Eliminate \( t \): from (1), \( t = (v - v_0)/a \). Substituting into (2) and simplifying gives
\[ v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0). \qquad (3) \]
4. Eliminate \( a \): from (1), \( at = v - v_0 \); then (2) becomes \( x - x_0 = v_0 t + \tfrac12 (v - v_0)t \), that is,
\[ x - x_0 = \tfrac12 (v_0 + v)\,t. \qquad (4) \]

Equation (4) says that for constant acceleration the average velocity is the mean of the initial and final velocities, because \( v(t) \) is linear in \( t \). For non-constant acceleration this is false in general.

**Choosing an equation.** Each equation omits exactly one of the five quantities \( \Delta x, v_0, v, a, t \): (1) omits \( \Delta x \), (2) omits \( v \), (3) omits \( t \), (4) omits \( a \). List what is known and what is asked; the equation that omits the quantity you neither know nor want is the one to use. Fix a positive direction first and give every vector quantity its sign.

**Worked example.** A car moving at 25.0 m/s brakes with constant acceleration of magnitude 6.00 m/s². How far does it travel while stopping, and how long does it take? What is the stopping distance if the driver first takes 0.80 s to react?

1. Positive direction: the car's motion. So \( v_0 = +25.0 \) m/s, \( a = -6.00 \) m/s², \( v = 0 \).
2. Distance, time not needed: use (3). \( 0 = 25.0^2 + 2(-6.00)\Delta x \), so \( \Delta x = 625/12.0 = 52.1 \) m.
3. Time: use (1). \( 0 = 25.0 - 6.00t \), so \( t = 4.17 \) s.
4. During the reaction time the car moves at constant speed: \( 25.0 \times 0.80 = 20.0 \) m. Total: \( 72.1 \) m.

The stopping distance scales as \( v_0^2 \): doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance, while the reaction distance only doubles.

**Common mistakes.** First, using these equations when \( a \) varies. If \( a(t) = 6t \), no single value of \( a \) makes (2) correct; you must integrate. Second, sign errors: writing \( a = +6.00 \) m/s² for a braking car in a coordinate system where the motion is positive gives \( \Delta x = -52.1 \) m, a nonsensical answer that is the signal to recheck signs. Third, in (3), a negative \( v^2 \) on the right side means the body never reaches that position; for example, a car braking from 25.0 m/s never reaches 60 m beyond its starting point.

questions.prompt: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.50 m/s². How far, in meters, has it traveled when its speed reaches 20.0 m/s?
questions.why: Time is neither given nor asked, so use \( v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x \): \( 20.0^2 = 0 + 2(2.50)\Delta x \), so \( \Delta x = 400/5.00 = 80.0 \) m.

questions.prompt: A vehicle moving at speed \( v_0 \) brakes with constant deceleration of magnitude \( b \). Give its stopping distance in terms of \( v_0 \) (type `v0`) and \( b \).
questions.why: With the motion positive, \( a = -b \) and final \( v = 0 \): \( 0 = v_0^2 - 2b\,\Delta x \), so \( \Delta x = v_0^2/(2b) \).

sections.title: Motion with constant acceleration

sections.md:
The most important constant-acceleration motion is **free fall**: motion under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected. This section applies the previous equations to it and then to problems in which two bodies must be at the same place at the same time.

**Free fall.** Near Earth's surface, every body moving under gravity alone has the same downward acceleration of magnitude \( g \), independent of its mass; we use \( g = 9.80 \) m/s². (The measured value varies from about 9.78 to 9.83 m/s² with latitude and altitude.) If you choose the \( y \)-axis pointing up, then \( a_y = -g \) throughout the flight, whether the body is rising, at the top, or falling. The equations of the previous section become
\[ v_y = v_{0y} - gt, \qquad y = y_0 + v_{0y}t - \tfrac12 g t^2, \qquad v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g(y - y_0). \]
Here \( g \) is a positive number; the minus signs come from the choice "up is positive".

**Worked example.** A ball is thrown straight up at 15.0 m/s from the edge of a cliff 20.0 m above the ground below; it misses the edge on the way down. Take up as positive with \( y_0 = 0 \) at the launch point, and \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².

1. Maximum height above launch: at the top \( v_y = 0 \), so \( 0 = 15.0^2 - 2(9.80)y_{\max} \), giving \( y_{\max} = 225/19.6 = 11.5 \) m.
2. Time to reach the ground, where \( y = -20.0 \) m: \( -20.0 = 15.0t - 4.90t^2 \), so \( 4.90t^2 - 15.0t - 20.0 = 0 \). The quadratic formula gives \( t = \big(15.0 + \sqrt{225 + 392}\big)/9.80 = 4.07 \) s; the other root is negative and describes a fictitious earlier time before launch.
3. Velocity on arrival: \( v_y = 15.0 - 9.80(4.065) = -24.8 \) m/s. As a check, \( v_y^2 = 225 + 2(9.80)(20.0) = 617 \), and \( \sqrt{617} = 24.8 \).

**Two moving objects.** To find where and when two bodies meet, write both positions in the same coordinate system as functions of the same clock, then set them equal. For example: a car passes a stationary police car at a constant 24.0 m/s; at that instant the police car starts from rest with constant acceleration 4.00 m/s². With the origin at the police car and \( t = 0 \) at the passing moment, \( x_{\text{car}} = 24.0t \) and \( x_{\text{police}} = 2.00t^2 \). Setting them equal gives \( t(2.00t - 24.0) = 0 \): \( t = 0 \) (the passing moment) or \( t = 12.0 \) s, at \( x = 288 \) m. The police car is then moving at \( 4.00 \times 12.0 = 48.0 \) m/s, twice the car's speed, which is what equation (4) predicts: equal displacements in equal times require equal average velocities, and the police car's average is \( (0 + 48.0)/2 = 24.0 \) m/s.

The plot shows both positions against time (horizontal axis \( t \)); the curves cross where the police car catches up.

```plot
x: 0, 15
y: 0, 400
xlabel: t (s)
ylabel: x (m)
f: 24*x | car, constant velocity
f: 2*x^2 | police car, constant acceleration
point: 12, 288
```

**Common mistakes.** Saying the acceleration is zero at the top of the flight: the velocity is zero there, but \( a_y = -g \) at every instant, which is why the ball comes back down. Using \( a = +9.80 \) m/s² with up positive: this silently treats gravity as pointing up. In two-object problems, using different origins or different starting times for the two bodies without converting to a common one.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 12.0 m/s. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s² and neglecting air resistance, how long, in seconds, until it returns to the launch height?
questions.why: Up positive: \( 0 = 12.0t - 4.90t^2 \), so \( t = 0 \) or \( t = 12.0/4.90 = 2.45 \) s. Equivalently, the rise takes \( v_0/g = 1.22 \) s and the fall takes the same time.

questions.prompt: A car passes a stationary police car at a constant 35.0 m/s. At that instant the police car starts from rest with constant acceleration 5.00 m/s². After how many seconds does it catch the car?
questions.why: Common origin and clock: \( x_{\text{car}} = 35.0t \), \( x_{\text{police}} = 2.50t^2 \). Equal when \( t(2.50t - 35.0) = 0 \), so \( t = 14.0 \) s (at \( x = 490 \) m).

phy-0-1.intro:
A thrown ball, a jet of water, a long jumper and a package released from an aircraft all follow curved paths. The question this chapter answers is how to predict such a path exactly: where the body will be at each moment, how high it will rise, where it will land, and how fast it will be moving when it does.

The answer rests on one structural fact. Near Earth's surface, and with air resistance neglected, the only acceleration is the constant gravitational acceleration, pointing straight down. The horizontal part of the motion is therefore unaccelerated and the vertical part is free fall, and these two one-dimensional motions proceed independently, linked only by the common clock. Projectile motion is thus the previous chapter applied twice. Before doing that you need the vector language for motion in a plane; once it is in place, the curved path, its range and its dependence on launch angle all follow by calculation rather than by memorized rules.

For \( \cos\theta_0 \ne 0 \), \( t = x/(v_0\cos\theta_0) \), so \( y = x\tan\theta_0 - \dfrac{g x^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta_0} \). The first term is the height of the straight line along the launch direction, where the body would be without gravity; the second is \( \tfrac12 g t^2 \) expressed in terms of \( x \), the distance fallen below that line. At \( \theta_0 = 90^\circ \), \( v_{0x} = 0 \), so \( x = 0 \) for all \( t \): \( t \) cannot be expressed through \( x \), there is no function \( y(x) \), and the motion is one-dimensional vertical free fall.

Its horizontal component therefore depends on \( v_y \) and its vertical component on \( v_x \), so \( dv_x/dt \) and \( dv_y/dt \) are no longer separate equations. Consequences: the projectile loses horizontal speed continuously, so the range and the maximum height are reduced; and because it is moving more slowly on the way down, the descent is steeper and the path is not symmetric about the apex. practice.why: \( \vec v = 5\,\hat{\imath} + (12 - 9.8t)\,\hat{\jmath} \), so \( |\vec v| = \sqrt{25 + (12 - 9.8t)^2} \). Its minimum, 5 m/s, occurs at the apex.

phy-0-1.scope: Motion in a vertical plane under constant gravitational acceleration with air resistance neglected: position, velocity and acceleration vectors, independence of components, time of flight, maximum height, trajectory, range, and launches to a different height; drag is discussed only qualitatively, and forces are left to the next chapter.

sections.md:
A body moving in a plane needs two numbers to locate it, so the one-dimensional definitions must be extended. This section does that with vectors and shows that each vector equation is simply a pair of one-dimensional equations.

**Definitions.** Fix axes: \( x \) horizontal and \( y \) vertical (upward), with unit vectors \( \hat{\imath} \) and \( \hat{\jmath} \). The **position vector** is
\[ \vec r(t) = x(t)\,\hat{\imath} + y(t)\,\hat{\jmath}. \]
The **velocity vector** and **acceleration vector** are its derivatives:
\[ \vec v = \frac{d\vec r}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dt}\hat{\imath} + \frac{dy}{dt}\hat{\jmath}, \qquad \vec a = \frac{d\vec v}{dt} = \frac{dv_x}{dt}\hat{\imath} + \frac{dv_y}{dt}\hat{\jmath}. \]
Because the unit vectors are constant, differentiating a vector means differentiating each component separately. The speed is the magnitude \( |\vec v| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} \), and the direction of motion is given by the angle \( \phi \) with \( \tan\phi = v_y/v_x \) (checking the quadrant from the signs of the components).

**Why velocity is tangent to the path.** Over a short interval the displacement \( \Delta\vec r \) is a chord of the path. As \( \Delta t \to 0 \) the chord's direction approaches the tangent direction, and \( \Delta\vec r/\Delta t \) approaches \( \vec v \). So the velocity always points along the path, in the direction of travel. The acceleration has no such restriction: it can point anywhere, and in projectile motion it points straight down while the path curves.

**Worked example.** A particle has \( \vec r(t) = (3.0t)\,\hat{\imath} + (4.0t - 4.9t^2)\,\hat{\jmath} \) in meters, with \( t \) in seconds.

1. Velocity: \( \vec v = 3.0\,\hat{\imath} + (4.0 - 9.8t)\,\hat{\jmath} \) m/s.
2. Acceleration: \( \vec a = -9.8\,\hat{\jmath} \) m/s², constant and downward. This is a projectile.
3. At \( t = 0.50 \) s: \( \vec v = 3.0\,\hat{\imath} - 0.90\,\hat{\jmath} \) m/s. Speed: \( \sqrt{3.0^2 + 0.90^2} = 3.13 \) m/s. Direction: \( \tan\phi = -0.90/3.0 \), so the velocity points \( 16.7^\circ \) below the horizontal. The particle is past its highest point, since \( v_y < 0 \).

**Common mistake.** Adding magnitudes instead of vectors: the speed is not \( |v_x| + |v_y| \) (here that would give 3.9 m/s). The components are perpendicular, so the magnitude comes from the Pythagorean theorem. A second mistake is reading the angle from \( \arctan(v_y/v_x) \) without checking signs; a velocity with \( v_x < 0 \) points into the second or third quadrant, which the calculator's arctangent never returns.

questions.prompt: A particle has \( \vec r(t) = (2.0t^2)\,\hat{\imath} + (3.0t - t^3)\,\hat{\jmath} \) (meters, seconds). Find its speed at \( t = 2.0 \) s, in m/s.

questions.model: The displacement \( \Delta\vec r \) over a short interval is the chord joining two nearby points of the path. As \( \Delta t \to 0 \), the chord's direction approaches the direction of the tangent line, so \( \vec v = \lim \Delta\vec r/\Delta t \) is tangent to the path. The acceleration is the rate of change of \( \vec v \); it records changes in direction as well as in magnitude, so it has no reason to point along the path. At the highest point of a projectile's path, \( \vec v = v_{0x}\hat{\imath} \) is horizontal while \( \vec a = -g\hat{\jmath} \) is vertical: perpendicular.
questions.prompt: Explain why the velocity vector of a particle is always tangent to its path, while the acceleration vector need not be. Give a concrete motion in which the acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity at some instant.
rubric: Velocity is the limit of Δr/Δt, and Δr is a chord that approaches the tangent direction
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which can change in direction as well as magnitude, so it is not tied to the path direction
Gives a valid example, such as a projectile at its highest point (v horizontal, a vertical)
questions.why: Tangency is a consequence of the definition as a limit of chords; acceleration measures turning as well as speeding up, which is why it points toward the inside of a curving path.

sections.title: Position, velocity, and acceleration as vectors

sections.md:
This section states the model precisely and shows why it turns a curved-path problem into two straight-line problems.

**The model.** A **projectile** is a body that, after launch, moves under gravity alone. We assume (i) air resistance is negligible, (ii) the region is small enough that \( g \) is constant in magnitude and direction, and (iii) the body can be treated as a particle. Then
\[ \vec a = -g\,\hat{\jmath}, \qquad a_x = 0, \quad a_y = -g, \]
with \( g = 9.80 \) m/s² and the \( y \)-axis upward.

**Independence of the components.** Because the acceleration vector has components \( (0, -g) \), and differentiation acts componentwise, the \( x \)-equation \( dv_x/dt = 0 \) contains nothing about \( y \), and the \( y \)-equation \( dv_y/dt = -g \) contains nothing about \( x \). Each can be integrated on its own with the constant-acceleration results from one-dimensional kinematics:
\[ x = x_0 + v_{0x}t, \qquad v_x = v_{0x}, \]
\[ y = y_0 + v_{0y}t - \tfrac12 g t^2, \qquad v_y = v_{0y} - gt. \]
The only thing the two motions share is the time \( t \). A problem typically uses one component to find \( t \) and the other to use it.

**Resolving the launch velocity.** If the body is launched with speed \( v_0 \) at angle \( \theta_0 \) above the horizontal, the **launch angle**, then
\[ v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta_0, \qquad v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta_0. \]

**Worked example (horizontal launch).** A ball rolls off a horizontal table 1.20 m high at 2.50 m/s. Where does it land, and with what vertical velocity? Put the origin on the floor directly below the edge.

1. Components: \( v_{0x} = 2.50 \) m/s, \( v_{0y} = 0 \), \( y_0 = 1.20 \) m.
2. Vertical motion determines the time: \( 0 = 1.20 - 4.90t^2 \), so \( t = \sqrt{1.20/4.90} = 0.495 \) s.
3. Horizontal motion uses that time: \( x = 2.50 \times 0.495 = 1.24 \) m from the foot of the table.
4. Vertical velocity at landing: \( v_y = -9.80 \times 0.495 = -4.85 \) m/s, while \( v_x \) is still 2.50 m/s.

Note that the fall time, 0.495 s, is exactly the time a ball dropped from rest at 1.20 m would take. The horizontal velocity does not delay or hasten the fall.

**Common mistake.** Believing that a faster horizontal launch "keeps the ball up" longer. In the drag-free model, the time to fall a given height depends only on \( v_{0y} \) and the height; a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height at the same instant land together. (With air resistance the components are coupled, because drag depends on the total speed; this is one reason the model is an approximation.) A second mistake is using \( v_0 \) itself, rather than its component, in one of the component equations.

questions.prompt: An aircraft flying horizontally at 60.0 m/s at an altitude of 180 m releases a package. Neglecting air resistance and using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², how far horizontally, in meters, does the package travel before reaching the ground?
questions.why: The package leaves with the aircraft's velocity: \( v_{0x} = 60.0 \) m/s, \( v_{0y} = 0 \). Vertical: \( 180 = 4.90t^2 \), \( t = 6.06 \) s. Horizontal: \( x = 60.0 \times 6.06 = 364 \) m.

So both reach \( y = 0 \) at the same time \( t = \sqrt{2y_0/g} \); they land simultaneously, with B a distance \( 3.0t \) farther from the table. This relies on the acceleration being exactly \( -g\hat{\jmath} \), i.e. on neglecting air resistance, which would depend on the total speed and so would couple the horizontal and vertical motions.
questions.prompt: Two identical balls leave the edge of a table at the same instant: A is simply released from rest, B is pushed off horizontally at 3.0 m/s. Which reaches the floor first? Justify from the component equations, and name the assumption on which your answer depends.

The y-equation y = y₀ − ½gt² does not contain vₓ, so the landing time is the same
They land simultaneously; B lands farther out

sections.title: The projectile model: independent components

sections.md:
With the component equations in hand, the natural questions are how long the projectile rises, how high it goes, and what curve it traces. This section answers all three for a launch from the origin at speed \( v_0 \) and angle \( \theta_0 \).

**The apex.** The highest point, the **apex**, is where the vertical velocity changes sign: \( v_y = 0 \). The horizontal velocity is unchanged there, so the velocity at the apex is \( v_{0x}\hat{\imath} \), not zero. From \( 0 = v_0\sin\theta_0 - gt \),
\[ t_{\text{top}} = \frac{v_0\sin\theta_0}{g}. \]
Substituting into the \( y \)-equation, or using \( v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g\,\Delta y \) with \( v_y = 0 \),
\[ H = \frac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta_0}{2g}. \]

**Flight time on level ground.** Setting \( y = 0 \): \( t\big(v_0\sin\theta_0 - \tfrac12 g t\big) = 0 \), so the landing time is
\[ T = \frac{2v_0\sin\theta_0}{g} = 2t_{\text{top}}. \]
The descent takes as long as the ascent, a consequence of the symmetry of the vertical motion about \( t_{\text{top}} \).

**The trajectory.** To get the path as a curve \( y(x) \), eliminate \( t \): from \( x = v_0\cos\theta_0\,t \), \( t = x/(v_0\cos\theta_0) \). Substituting,
\[ y = x\tan\theta_0 - \frac{g}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta_0}\,x^2. \]
This is a quadratic in \( x \) with negative leading coefficient: the **trajectory** is a downward-opening parabola. The linear term alone would be the straight line along the launch direction; the quadratic term is how far the body has fallen below that line, \( \tfrac12 g t^2 \), rewritten in terms of \( x \).

**Worked example.** A ball is launched from level ground at 20.0 m/s, 35.0° above the horizontal; \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².

1. Components: \( v_{0x} = 20.0\cos 35.0^\circ = 16.38 \) m/s, \( v_{0y} = 20.0\sin 35.0^\circ = 11.47 \) m/s.
2. Time to apex: \( 11.47/9.80 = 1.17 \) s.
3. Maximum height: \( 11.47^2/(2 \times 9.80) = 6.71 \) m.
4. Flight time: \( 2t_{\text{top}} = 2.341 \) s; horizontal distance \( 16.383 \times 2.341 = 38.4 \) m (carry unrounded intermediate values: \( 16.38 \times 2.34 \) would give 38.3 m).

The plot draws this trajectory parametrically (horizontal axis \( x \), vertical axis \( y \), both in meters) and marks the apex.

```plot
x: 0, 42
y: 0, 12
xlabel: x (m)
ylabel: y (m)
param: 16.383*t; 11.472*t - 4.9*t^2 | trajectory
t: 0, 2.341
point: 19.18, 6.714
```

**Common mistakes.** Setting the velocity to zero at the apex; only its vertical component vanishes. Using the level-ground flight time \( T = 2v_0\sin\theta_0/g \) when the landing point is higher or lower than the launch point; that formula came from setting \( y = 0 \) and is valid only there. Mixing degrees and radians on a calculator when evaluating \( \sin\theta_0 \).

\( \vec v = 0 \) and \( \vec a = -g\hat{\jmath} \)
\( \vec v = v_0\cos\theta_0\,\hat{\imath} \) and \( \vec a = -g\hat{\jmath} \)
\( \vec v = v_0\cos\theta_0\,\hat{\imath} \) and \( \vec a = 0 \)

sections.title: Time to the apex, maximum height, and the shape of the path

sections.md:
Gunners asked this question long before calculus, and Galileo's *Two New Sciences* (1638) answered it for the drag-free case: at a given launch speed, which angle carries the projectile farthest over level ground? This section derives the range and answers it.

**The range formula.** The **horizontal range** \( R \) is the horizontal distance traveled when the projectile returns to its launch height. Multiply the horizontal velocity by the flight time from the previous section:
\[ R = v_0\cos\theta_0 \cdot \frac{2v_0\sin\theta_0}{g} = \frac{v_0^2\,2\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0}{g} = \frac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta_0}{g}, \]
using the double-angle identity \( \sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \).

**Maximum range.** For fixed \( v_0 \), \( R \) is largest when \( \sin 2\theta_0 \) is largest, which is 1, at \( 2\theta_0 = 90^\circ \), i.e. \( \theta_0 = 45^\circ \). The maximum range is \( R_{\max} = v_0^2/g \).

**Complementary angles.** Since \( \sin(180^\circ - \alpha) = \sin\alpha \), the angles \( \theta_0 \) and \( 90^\circ - \theta_0 \) give
\[ \sin 2(90^\circ - \theta_0) = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta_0) = \sin 2\theta_0, \]
hence equal ranges. The higher launch spends longer in the air (larger \( v_{0y} \)) but moves more slowly horizontally (smaller \( v_{0x} \)), and the two effects cancel exactly. The paths are different: the steeper one rises higher.

**Worked example.** At \( v_0 = 20.0 \) m/s and \( g = 9.80 \) m/s²:
1. \( \theta_0 = 35.0^\circ \): \( R = 400\sin 70.0^\circ/9.80 = 38.4 \) m, matching the previous section's step-by-step result.
2. \( \theta_0 = 55.0^\circ \): \( \sin 110^\circ = \sin 70^\circ \), so again \( R = 38.4 \) m.
3. \( \theta_0 = 45.0^\circ \): \( R = 400/9.80 = 40.8 \) m, the maximum.

In the plot, drag the slider \( a \) (the launch angle in degrees, launch speed fixed at 20.0 m/s). Watch the vertical line marking the landing point: it moves outward as \( a \) rises toward 45, then back in. Setting \( a \) to 35 and then 55 lands the ball at the same point along visibly different arcs.

```plot
x: 0, 45
y: 0, 21
xlabel: x (m)
ylabel: y (m)
slider: a, 5, 85, 35 | launch angle (degrees)
param: 20*cos(a*pi/180)*t; 20*sin(a*pi/180)*t - 4.9*t^2 | trajectory, v0 = 20 m/s
t: 0, 4.1
vline: 400*sin(2*a*pi/180)/9.8 | landing point
```

(The curve is drawn for a fixed time window and so continues below ground level after landing; only the part above the axis is physical.)

**Common mistakes.** Applying \( R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta_0/g \) when launch and landing heights differ; its derivation used \( y = 0 \) at landing. Concluding that 45° is always optimal: for a launch from above the landing level (a shot put released at shoulder height), the best angle is below 45°, and air resistance generally lowers it further.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum launch speed, in m/s, that allows a projectile to reach a target 60.0 m away on level ground? Use \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².
questions.why: For a given speed the greatest range is \( v_0^2/g \), at 45°. The minimum speed satisfies \( v_0^2/g = 60.0 \), so \( v_0 = \sqrt{588} = 24.2 \) m/s.

questions.model: Assume no air resistance, constant \( g \), and landing at the launch height. Then \( T = 2v_0\sin\theta_0/g \) and \( R = v_0\cos\theta_0\,T = v_0^2\sin 2\theta_0/g \). For the complementary angle, \( \sin 2(90^\circ - \theta_0) = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta_0) = \sin 2\theta_0 \), so the ranges agree. For \( 0^\circ < \theta_0 < 90^\circ \), \( 2\theta_0 \in (0^\circ, 180^\circ) \) and \( \sin 2\theta_0 \le 1 \), with equality only at \( 2\theta_0 = 90^\circ \); hence the unique maximum is at \( \theta_0 = 45^\circ \), with \( R_{\max} = v_0^2/g \).

rubric: Derives or quotes R = v₀² sin 2θ₀/g from R = v₀ₓ · T with T = 2v₀ sin θ₀ / g
Shows sin 2(90° − θ₀) = sin(180° − 2θ₀) = sin 2θ₀
Maximum of sin 2θ₀ on 0° to 90° is 1 at θ₀ = 45°
Assumptions: no air resistance, constant g, landing at launch height, same v₀
questions.why: Each assumption is used: drag would change the component equations, and a different landing height would change \( T \).

sections.title: Range on level ground and the best launch angle

sections.md:
Real launches rarely land at their starting height. This section handles the general case, shows how to get the velocity at impact, and states what the drag-free model leaves out.

**General procedure.** Place the origin at the launch point with \( y \) up. The landing condition is \( y = y_{\text{land}} \), a known number (negative if the landing point is below the launch point). The vertical equation
\[ y_{\text{land}} = v_{0y}t - \tfrac12 g t^2 \]
is a quadratic in \( t \). It has two roots; the physical one is the positive root that describes the body arriving at that height after launch (for a landing point below the launch, the other root is negative and describes a fictitious earlier time on the extended parabola). Then \( x = v_{0x}t \) gives the horizontal distance.

**Impact velocity.** At the landing time, \( v_x = v_{0x} \) and \( v_y = v_{0y} - gt \); the speed is \( \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} \) and the angle below the horizontal is \( \arctan(|v_y|/v_x) \). A useful check comes from the time-free equation of one-dimensional kinematics applied to the vertical motion: \( v_y^2 = v_{0y}^2 - 2g\,\Delta y \), so
\[ v^2 = v_{0x}^2 + v_{0y}^2 - 2g\,\Delta y = v_0^2 - 2g\,\Delta y. \]
The speed at a given height depends only on the launch speed and the drop, not on the launch angle. (The chapter on energy will explain this as conservation of mechanical energy.)

**Worked example.** A stone is thrown from the top of a 25.0 m cliff at 18.0 m/s, 30.0° above the horizontal, and lands on flat ground below; \( g = 9.80 \) m/s².

1. Components: \( v_{0x} = 18.0\cos 30.0^\circ = 15.59 \) m/s, \( v_{0y} = 9.00 \) m/s.
2. Landing: \( -25.0 = 9.00t - 4.90t^2 \), i.e. \( 4.90t^2 - 9.00t - 25.0 = 0 \), so
\[ t = \frac{9.00 + \sqrt{81.0 + 490}}{9.80} = 3.357 \text{ s}. \]
3. Horizontal distance: \( 15.59 \times 3.357 = 52.3 \) m.
4. Impact: \( v_y = 9.00 - 9.80(3.357) = -23.9 \) m/s, speed \( \sqrt{15.59^2 + 23.9^2} = 28.5 \) m/s at \( \arctan(23.9/15.59) = 56.9^\circ \) below the horizontal.
5. Check: \( v^2 = 18.0^2 + 2(9.80)(25.0) = 814 \), and \( \sqrt{814} = 28.5 \) m/s.

**Limits of the model.** The drag-free model is excellent for dense, slow bodies over short distances (a thrown stone, a ball rolling off a table) and poor for light or fast ones (a badminton shuttle, a long drive in golf, artillery). **Air resistance** acts opposite to the velocity and grows with speed. It reduces both height and range, makes the descent steeper and horizontally shorter than the ascent (the path is no longer a parabola), and couples the components. For realistic projectiles with drag, the angle of maximum range is generally below 45°; how far below depends on the body and speed, and no simple formula gives it.

**Common mistakes.** Taking the negative root of the quadratic, or the root for the wrong crossing when the target is above the launch point (then both roots may be positive: one on the way up, one on the way down, and the problem statement decides which is meant). Using \( y_{\text{land}} = +25.0 \) m for a landing point below the launch point while keeping \( y \) upward.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown from the roof of a 10.0 m tall building at 15.0 m/s, 40.0° above the horizontal, and lands on level ground. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², how far from the base of the building does it land, in meters?
A ball is thrown at 12.0 m/s, 25.0° above the horizontal, from a platform 8.00 m above level ground. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find its speed just before it lands, in m/s.
questions.why: \( v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g\,\Delta y = 144 + 2(9.80)(8.00) = 300.8 \), so \( v = 17.3 \) m/s. The launch angle does not enter; computing components (\( v_x = 10.88 \), \( v_y = -13.51 \) m/s at landing) gives the same result.

phy-0-2.intro:
Kinematics, developed in the previous two chapters, describes motion completely once the acceleration is known, but it says nothing about what the acceleration will be. Why does a released stone speed up, a sliding book slow down, a rope pull harder on one crate than on another? Mechanics needed a rule connecting the acceleration of a body to its surroundings.

Newton's three laws of motion supply that rule. The surroundings act on a body through **forces**; the net force fixes the acceleration through the second law; and every force is one half of an interaction between two bodies, which is the content of the third law. Applying the laws in practice depends on one disciplined habit: isolating a single body and accounting for every force exerted on it, which is what a free-body diagram does. This chapter builds the laws in order, then uses them on bodies at rest, in accelerating elevators, and joined by ropes and pulleys.

sections.md:
Kinematics describes motion but does not explain it: given \( x(t) \) we can compute the acceleration, but nothing so far tells us what the acceleration will be. This section introduces the quantity that determines it, force, and the first of Newton's laws, which says what happens when the forces on a body balance.

**Force and net force.** A **force** is a push or a pull exerted on a body by another body, either by contact (a hand, a rope, a floor) or at a distance (Earth's gravity). Forces are vectors: each has a magnitude, measured in newtons (N, defined in the next section), and a direction. Experiment shows that several forces acting on one body together have the same effect as a single force equal to their vector sum, the **net force**:
\[ \vec F_{\text{net}} = \sum_i \vec F_i, \qquad F_{\text{net},x} = \sum_i F_{i,x}, \quad F_{\text{net},y} = \sum_i F_{i,y}. \]
Which forces count depends on what you call the body. Once a **system** is chosen, an **external force** is one exerted on it by something outside it, and an **internal force** is one exerted by one part of the system on another. Only external forces change the motion of the system as a whole; the reason, Newton's third law, is given in a later section.

**The first law.**

> **Newton's first law.** If the net external force on a body is zero, the body remains at rest if it is at rest, and keeps moving with constant velocity (constant speed in a straight line) if it is moving.

In symbols, \( \vec F_{\text{net}} = \vec 0 \) implies that \( \vec v \) is constant. A change of velocity, in magnitude or in direction, requires a nonzero net force. The tendency of a body to keep its velocity is called **inertia**. A book sliding across a table slows down not because motion runs out but because friction, a force, acts on it; on smoother surfaces it slides farther, and in the frictionless limit it would slide at constant velocity indefinitely.

A body with zero acceleration is in **equilibrium**, and by the first law this happens exactly when \( \vec F_{\text{net}} = \vec 0 \). A parked car and a car cruising at a steady 25 m/s along a straight road are both in equilibrium.

**Inertial frames.** Velocity is measured relative to a reference frame, and the first law cannot hold in every frame. A passenger standing in a bus that brakes hard lurches forward, although nothing pushes her forward: relative to the bus she accelerates with no net force on her. The first law therefore also serves as a criterion: an **inertial reference frame** is one in which a body with zero net force moves with constant velocity. A frame moving with constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial; a frame that accelerates or rotates relative to one is not. The ground is not exactly inertial, since Earth rotates, but a point on the equator has a centripetal acceleration of only about 0.034 m/s², so in this course the ground frame is treated as inertial. The first and second laws hold only in inertial frames, and every analysis in this course is carried out in one.

**Worked example.** Two horizontal forces act on a puck on frictionless ice: \( \vec F_1 \) of 12.0 N along \( +x \), and \( \vec F_2 \) of 8.0 N at \( 120^\circ \) from the \( +x \)-axis. (The vertical forces, weight and the push of the ice, balance and are omitted.) Find the net force and the one additional force that would put the puck in equilibrium.

1. Components: \( \vec F_2 = 8.0(\cos 120^\circ,\ \sin 120^\circ) = (-4.0,\ 6.93) \) N.
2. Sum: \( \vec F_{\text{net}} = (12.0 - 4.0,\ 0 + 6.93) = (8.0,\ 6.93) \) N.
3. Magnitude \( \sqrt{8.0^2 + 6.93^2} = 10.6 \) N, at \( \arctan(6.93/8.0) = 40.9^\circ \) above the \( +x \)-axis.
4. Equilibrium needs a third force \( \vec F_3 = -\vec F_{\text{net}} = (-8.0,\ -6.93) \) N: 10.6 N at \( 220.9^\circ \).

**Common mistakes.** Believing that motion requires a force in the direction of motion: a force is needed to change the velocity, not to maintain it. Adding force magnitudes instead of vectors: 12.0 N and 8.0 N combine to 20.0 N only if they point the same way.

An inertial reference frame is one in which a body with zero net force moves with constant velocity. The bus, while braking, accelerates relative to the ground; measured in the bus frame, the passenger accelerates forward although no force produces that acceleration, so the first law fails there and the bus frame is non-inertial. sections.title: Forces and the first law

sections.md:
The first law says what happens when the net force is zero. The second law says what happens when it is not, and it is the equation from which nearly every problem in mechanics starts.

> **Newton's second law.** In an inertial frame, the acceleration of a body is in the direction of the net external force on it, proportional to that force and inversely proportional to the body's mass:
> \[ \vec F_{\text{net}} = \sum \vec F = m\vec a. \]

This is a vector equation, so it holds for each component separately:
\[ \sum F_x = m a_x, \qquad \sum F_y = m a_y, \qquad \sum F_z = m a_z. \]
That is what makes it usable: choose axes, resolve every force, and each axis gives one scalar equation. The acceleration always points along the net force; the velocity need not. A projectile at the top of its path moves horizontally while the net force on it is vertical.

**Mass and the newton.** The **mass** \( m \) of a body (SI unit: the kilogram) measures its inertia: the same net force gives twice the mass half the acceleration. The SI unit of force is fixed by the second law. One **newton** is the net force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²:
\[ 1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg·m/s}^2. \]
The second law is nevertheless not a mere definition of force. Forces can be identified and measured independently (with a calibrated spring, for instance), and the law asserts an experimentally verified relation among force, mass and acceleration that could have been otherwise. It applies to a particle, or to an extended body treated as one, whose parts all share a single acceleration.

**Weight.** The gravitational force that Earth exerts on a body is its **weight** \( \vec w \). In free fall this is the only force, and the body accelerates at \( g \) downward, so the second law gives
\[ w = mg, \]
directed downward, with \( g = 9.80 \) m/s² near Earth's surface. Mass and weight are different quantities. Mass is a property of the body, in kilograms, the same everywhere; weight is a force, in newtons, and depends on where the body is. An 80.0 kg astronaut weighs 784 N on Earth and \( 80.0 \times 1.62 = 130 \) N on the Moon, yet her mass is 80.0 kg in both places, and she is exactly as hard to set in horizontal motion on either.

**Worked example (constant force).** A 1500 kg car is driven forward by a 4500 N force from the road and resisted by 1500 N of air drag; the vertical forces balance. Along the road, \( \sum F_x = 4500 - 1500 = 3000 \) N, so \( a_x = 3000/1500 = 2.00 \) m/s².

**Forces that vary with time.** When the net force depends on time, the second law gives the acceleration at each instant, \( a_x(t) = F_x(t)/m \), and velocity and position follow by integration, as in one-dimensional kinematics:
\[ v_x(t) = v_{0x} + \frac{1}{m}\int_0^t F_x(t')\,dt', \qquad x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t v_x(t')\,dt'. \]
The constant-acceleration equations do not apply.

**Worked example (time-dependent force).** A 2.00 kg block starts from rest at \( x = 0 \) on a frictionless horizontal surface and is pulled by a horizontal force \( F_x = (6.00\ \text{N/s})\,t \).

1. \( a_x = F_x/m = 3.00t \) m/s².
2. \( v_x = \int_0^t 3.00t'\,dt' = 1.50t^2 \) m/s.
3. \( x = \int_0^t 1.50t'^2\,dt' = 0.500t^3 \) m.
4. At \( t = 2.00 \) s: \( v_x = 6.00 \) m/s and \( x = 4.00 \) m. Using \( x = \tfrac12 a t^2 \) with the final acceleration, 6.00 m/s², would give 12.0 m, three times too much.

The plot shows \( a_x(t) = 3t \) (in m/s², against \( t \) in s). The shaded area from 0 to 2 s is the velocity gained, 6.00 m/s.

```plot
x: 0, 3
y: 0, 10
xlabel: t (s)
ylabel: a (m/s²)
f: 3*x | a(t) = 3t
shade: 3*x, 0, 2 | area = v(2) = 6.00 m/s
```

**Common mistakes.** Treating \( m\vec a \) as one of the forces: it is the result of the forces, the right-hand side of the equation, never an arrow on the diagram. Stating a weight in kilograms. Assuming a body moves in the direction of the net force; it accelerates in that direction.

questions.prompt: A 3.00 kg block, initially at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface, is pulled by a horizontal force \( F(t) = (12.0\ \text{N/s}^2)\,t^2 \). Find its speed at \( t = 3.00 \) s, in m/s.
questions.why: \( a = F/m = 4.00t^2 \) m/s². Integrating from rest: \( v = \int_0^t 4.00t'^2\,dt' = \tfrac{4.00}{3}t^3 \). At \( t = 3.00 \) s: \( v = \tfrac{4.00}{3}(27.0) = 36.0 \) m/s. The acceleration is not constant, so \( v = at \) with \( a(3) = 36 \) m/s² (which would give 108 m/s) is wrong.

options: Her mass is 80.0 kg and her weight is 130 N.
Her mass is 13.2 kg and her weight is 130 N.
Her mass is 80.0 kg and her weight is 784 N.
Her mass is 80.0 kg and her weight is 80.0 kg.
questions.prompt: An astronaut whose mass on Earth is 80.0 kg stands on the Moon, where \( g = 1.62 \) m/s². Which statement is correct?
questions.why: Mass is a property of the body and does not change: 80.0 kg. Weight is the local gravitational force, \( mg = 80.0 \times 1.62 = 130 \) N. Option 2 scales the mass with \( g \) (treating mass as if it were weight); option 3 treats weight as intrinsic; option 4 uses the everyday habit of stating weight in kilograms, which confuses a force with a mass.

sections.title: The second law, mass, and weight

sections.md:
Forces arise from interactions between two bodies, and the third law says that every interaction acts both ways. This section states the law, shows how to find the partner of any force, and explains why partners never cancel in a second-law equation.

> **Newton's third law.** If body B exerts a force \( \vec F_{AB} \) on body A, then A exerts a force \( \vec F_{BA} \) on B, and
> \[ \vec F_{BA} = -\vec F_{AB}. \]

(Read \( \vec F_{AB} \) as "the force on A by B".) The two forces form an **interaction pair**, often called an action–reaction pair. The members of a pair:

1. have equal magnitudes and opposite directions;
2. act on different bodies, one on each;
3. are of the same physical type (both gravitational, both normal forces, both friction);
4. exist simultaneously; neither causes the other.

To find the partner of a force, describe it as "the force of type X on A by B" and swap the bodies: the partner is "the force of type X on B by A".

**Why partners do not cancel.** The second law for body A sums the forces on A. The partner of any force on A acts on B, so it never appears in A's equation. Forces cancel in a sum only when both act on the same body. The same fact explains why internal forces drop out of the net force on a system: when both A and B belong to the system, both members of each pair appear in the sum, and they add to zero.

**Pairs versus balanced forces.** A book rests on a table. Two forces act on it: its weight (Earth pulls it down) and the normal force (the table pushes it up). They are equal and opposite, but they are not a third-law pair. Both act on the same body, they are of different types, and their equality follows from the second law with \( \vec a = \vec 0 \); if the table were in an accelerating elevator they would differ. The partner of the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull on Earth, acting upward on Earth. The partner of the normal force is the book's downward push on the table.

**Worked example.** Two blocks, \( m_1 = 3.00 \) kg and \( m_2 = 2.00 \) kg, sit side by side on a frictionless floor. A horizontal force \( F = 20.0 \) N pushes block 1, which pushes block 2. Find the acceleration and the contact force \( P \) between the blocks.

1. The blocks move together, so they share one acceleration. Take both as the system: the contact forces are internal, and the only external horizontal force is \( F \). So \( a = F/(m_1 + m_2) = 20.0/5.00 = 4.00 \) m/s².
2. Block 2 alone: the only horizontal force on it is the push of block 1, so \( P = m_2 a = (2.00)(4.00) = 8.00 \) N.
3. Block 1 alone: \( F \) forward and, by the third law, block 2's push of 8.00 N backward. Check: \( 20.0 - 8.00 = 12.0 \) N \( = m_1 a \).

The contact force is smaller than \( F \): block 1 transmits only the force needed to accelerate block 2. If the same 20.0 N pushed block 2 instead, the contact force would be \( m_1 a = 12.0 \) N.

**Common mistakes.** Calling weight and normal force a third-law pair. Arguing that a horse cannot pull a cart because the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Those two forces act on different bodies. The cart accelerates if the horse's forward pull on it exceeds the resistance acting on the cart; the horse accelerates if the ground's forward push on its hooves exceeds the cart's backward pull on the horse. Nothing requires either net force to be zero.

questions.model: (a) Two forces act on the book: its weight \( mg \), exerted downward by Earth, and the normal force \( N \), exerted upward by the table. (b) The partner of the weight is the gravitational force of the book on Earth, of magnitude \( mg \), directed upward and acting on Earth. The partner of the normal force is the contact force of the book on the table, of magnitude \( N \), directed downward and acting on the table. (c) The book is at rest, so \( a = 0 \) and the second law gives \( N - mg = 0 \). This equality comes from the book's state of motion, not from the third law: the two forces act on the same body and are of different types (gravitational and contact). If the table were in an elevator accelerating upward, \( N \) would exceed \( mg \), while each third-law pair would still consist of exactly equal and opposite forces.
questions.prompt: A book rests on a table in a room at rest. (a) List the forces acting on the book. (b) For each, name its third-law partner, stating the body it acts on. (c) Explain why the two forces on the book are equal in magnitude, and why that equality is not an instance of the third law.
rubric: (a) Weight (Earth on book, down) and normal force (table on book, up)
(b) Partner of the weight: book's gravitational pull on Earth, upward, acting on Earth; partner of the normal force: book's push on the table, downward, acting on the table
(c) Equality follows from the second law with a = 0 (net force on the book is zero)
They are not a pair: both act on the same body, they are of different types, and they would differ if the book accelerated vertically
questions.why: The test for a third-law pair is: two bodies, swapped roles, same type of force. Balanced forces on one body satisfy none of these.

questions.prompt: A horizontal force of 30.0 N pushes a 4.00 kg block, which in turn pushes a 6.00 kg block ahead of it across a frictionless floor. Find the magnitude of the force the 6.00 kg block exerts on the 4.00 kg block, in newtons.
questions.why: System of both blocks: \( a = 30.0/10.0 = 3.00 \) m/s². The only horizontal force on the 6.00 kg block is the push of the 4.00 kg block: \( P = (6.00)(3.00) = 18.0 \) N. By the third law the 6.00 kg block pushes back on the 4.00 kg block with 18.0 N. Check on the 4.00 kg block: \( 30.0 - 18.0 = 12.0 = (4.00)(3.00) \).

sections.title: The third law and interaction pairs

sections.md:
Weight is given by a formula. The contact forces are not: the push of a floor and the pull of a rope take whatever values the motion requires, and Newton's laws are how we find them. This section defines the two contact forces used in this chapter and the diagram that organizes every force problem. Surfaces here are frictionless; friction, the component of a contact force along the surface, is the subject of the next chapter.

**Normal force.** When a body presses against a surface, the surface pushes back perpendicular (normal) to itself. This **normal force** \( \vec N \) is a **constraint force**: it has no formula of its own, but takes whatever magnitude keeps the body from moving into the surface. A surface can push but not pull, so \( N \ge 0 \); if the equations demand \( N < 0 \), the body has left the surface. The normal force equals \( mg \) only in a special case: a horizontal surface, no other vertical forces, and no vertical acceleration.

**Tension.** A taut rope, string or cable pulls on a body attached to it, along the rope and away from the body. The magnitude of this pull is the **tension** \( T \). A rope can only pull, so \( T \ge 0 \). Apply the second law to a straight piece of rope with tensions \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) at its two ends, pulling in opposite directions: \( T_2 - T_1 = m_{\text{rope}}\,a \). For an **ideal rope**, massless and inextensible, \( m_{\text{rope}} = 0 \), so \( T_1 = T_2 \): the tension is the same all along the rope, whatever its acceleration. An **ideal pulley**, massless and frictionless, changes the direction of a rope without changing its tension.

**The free-body diagram.** A **free-body diagram** shows one body, isolated from its surroundings, with an arrow for every external force acting on it. The procedure:

1. Choose the body (or system) and draw it alone, as a dot or a simple outline.
2. Draw its weight \( m\vec g \), downward.
3. Go around the body: wherever something touches it, draw the contact force there, a normal force for each surface and a tension for each rope.
4. Draw any other identified force, such as an applied push, and label every arrow with the agent that exerts it.
5. Choose axes, one of them along the acceleration if its direction is known, and resolve each force that is not along an axis.
6. Write \( \sum F_x = ma_x \) and \( \sum F_y = ma_y \).

Every arrow must be a force on the chosen body by an identifiable agent. The diagram never contains forces the body exerts on other things, internal forces, the velocity, or \( m\vec a \).

**Worked example.** A 20.0 kg crate on a frictionless floor is pulled by a rope with tension 80.0 N directed \( 30.0^\circ \) above the horizontal. Find the normal force and the acceleration.

1. Diagram: weight \( mg = 196 \) N down; normal force \( N \) up; tension 80.0 N at \( 30.0^\circ \) above \( +x \). Axes: \( x \) along the floor (the direction of the acceleration), \( y \) up.
2. \( y \)-equation: the crate stays on the floor, so \( a_y = 0 \): \( N + 80.0\sin 30.0^\circ - 196 = 0 \), giving \( N = 196 - 40.0 = 156 \) N.
3. \( x \)-equation: \( 80.0\cos 30.0^\circ = (20.0)\,a_x \), giving \( a_x = 69.3/20.0 = 3.46 \) m/s².

The normal force is less than the weight because the rope's upward component supports part of the weight. The floor's push would fall to zero, and the crate would begin to lift, at \( T\sin 30.0^\circ = 196 \) N, that is \( T = 392 \) N.

**Common mistakes.** Writing \( N = mg \) out of habit. Drawing a force "of the throw" or "of motion" on a body that is no longer touching the thrower. Drawing both members of a third-law pair on one diagram; only the one acting on the chosen body belongs there.

questions.prompt: A 5.00 kg box on a frictionless horizontal floor is pushed with a force of 40.0 N directed \( 25.0^\circ \) below the horizontal. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the normal force of the floor on the box, in newtons.
questions.why: Vertical forces: \( N \) up, \( mg = 49.0 \) N down, and the push's vertical component \( 40.0\sin 25.0^\circ = 16.9 \) N down. With \( a_y = 0 \): \( N = 49.0 + 16.9 = 65.9 \) N. Pushing downward at an angle presses the box into the floor, so \( N > mg \).

questions.model: The 'force of the stick' does not exist once the puck has left the stick: a contact force acts only while there is contact, and every arrow on a free-body diagram must be a force exerted now by an identifiable agent. The student has drawn the velocity, or a remembered push, as a force. By the first law no force is needed to keep the puck moving; a force would be needed to change its velocity. The correct diagram has two arrows: the weight \( mg \) downward (Earth) and the normal force \( N \) upward (ice). With no vertical acceleration, \( N = mg \), the net force is zero, and the puck slides at constant velocity.
questions.prompt: A hockey puck slides across frictionless ice after leaving the stick. A student's free-body diagram of the puck shows three forces: its weight, the normal force from the ice, and a horizontal 'force of the stick' in the direction of motion. Identify the error, explain it with Newton's laws, and describe the correct diagram and what it predicts.
rubric: The stick is no longer in contact, so it exerts no force; every force needs an agent acting now
Motion does not require a force in its direction (first law)
Correct diagram: weight down and normal force up only
Net force zero, so the puck moves at constant velocity (N = mg here)
questions.why: The stick's push acted during contact and changed the puck's velocity then; afterwards it is part of the puck's history, not a present force.

sections.title: Normal force, tension, and the free-body diagram

sections.md:
Cables, supports and hanging loads are meant to stay at rest, and the practical question is how large the forces in them must be. For a body in equilibrium the second law with \( \vec a = \vec 0 \) answers it.

**Conditions.** A body is in (translational) equilibrium if and only if \( \sum\vec F = \vec 0 \), that is,
\[ \sum F_x = 0, \qquad \sum F_y = 0. \]
In a plane these are two independent scalar equations, so one body's diagram can determine at most two unknown force magnitudes. When there are more unknowns, draw a diagram for another body or for a point where several ropes meet. A knot joining ideal ropes is massless and therefore always has zero net force, so its diagram involves only the tensions.

**Worked example.** A 15.0 kg traffic light hangs from a vertical cable attached to a knot. The knot is held by two cables making \( 30.0^\circ \) (left) and \( 45.0^\circ \) (right) with the horizontal. Find the three tensions.

1. Light: \( T_3 - mg = 0 \), so \( T_3 = (15.0)(9.80) = 147 \) N.
2. Knot: \( T_1 \) up and to the left at \( 30.0^\circ \), \( T_2 \) up and to the right at \( 45.0^\circ \), \( T_3 = 147 \) N down:
\[ x:\ -T_1\cos 30.0^\circ + T_2\cos 45.0^\circ = 0, \qquad y:\ T_1\sin 30.0^\circ + T_2\sin 45.0^\circ - 147 = 0. \]
3. From \( x \): \( T_2 = T_1\cos 30.0^\circ/\cos 45.0^\circ = 1.225\,T_1 \). Substituting in \( y \): \( T_1(0.500 + 0.866) = 147 \), so \( T_1 = 108 \) N and \( T_2 = 132 \) N.

The horizontal components must balance, so the steeper cable, which has the smaller cosine, carries the larger tension. Note also that \( T_1 + T_2 = 240 \) N exceeds the 147 N weight: the cables do not simply divide the weight between them, because part of each tension is spent pulling horizontally against the other cable.

**General solution.** Solving the same two equations for cables at angles \( \theta_1 \) and \( \theta_2 \) above the horizontal, and using \( \sin\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2 = \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) \),
\[ T_1 = \frac{mg\cos\theta_2}{\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}, \qquad T_2 = \frac{mg\cos\theta_1}{\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}. \]

**The symmetric case.** With \( \theta_1 = \theta_2 = \theta \), each tension is \( T = mg/(2\sin\theta) \). As the cables flatten, \( \theta \to 0 \) and \( T \to \infty \): no finite tension can support a weight on a perfectly straight horizontal cable, since a horizontal cable has no vertical component. This is why power lines and clotheslines always sag. The plot shows \( T \) (in N) against \( \theta \) (in degrees) for the 147 N light, with the value \( mg/2 \) that holds only for vertical cables.

```plot
x: 0, 90
y: 0, 600
xlabel: θ (degrees)
ylabel: T (N)
f: 147/(2*sin(x*pi/180)) | tension in each cable
hline: 73.5 | mg/2
```

**Common mistakes.** Assuming that two cables share a weight equally, or have equal tensions when their angles differ. Using sine where cosine belongs when the angle is measured from the vertical rather than from the horizontal; decide from the diagram which component is adjacent to the given angle. Forgetting that the vertical cable's tension equals \( mg \) only because the light is at rest.

questions.prompt: A 10.0 kg sign hangs from a knot held by two cables, one at \( 40.0^\circ \) and one at \( 60.0^\circ \) above the horizontal. Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², find the tension in the \( 60.0^\circ \) cable, in newtons.
questions.why: Knot equations: \( T_{40}\cos 40.0^\circ = T_{60}\cos 60.0^\circ \) and \( T_{40}\sin 40.0^\circ + T_{60}\sin 60.0^\circ = 98.0 \) N. Solving, \( T_{60} = \dfrac{mg\cos 40.0^\circ}{\sin 100.0^\circ} = \dfrac{98.0(0.766)}{0.985} = 76.2 \) N (and \( T_{40} = 49.8 \) N). The steeper cable carries more.

questions.model: The midpoint is in equilibrium under the two cable tensions and the load. By symmetry the two tensions are equal, \( T \), and their horizontal components cancel. Vertically, each half contributes \( T\sin\theta \) upward, so \( 2T\sin\theta = mg \) and \( T = \dfrac{mg}{2\sin\theta} \). As the cable is pulled straighter, \( \theta \to 0 \), \( \sin\theta \to 0 \), and the required tension grows without bound. At \( \theta = 0 \) both tensions are horizontal and have no vertical component at all, so \( \sum F_y = -mg \ne 0 \) whatever \( T \) is: equilibrium is impossible. A supported load therefore always produces a sag, however taut the cable.
questions.prompt: A load of weight \( mg \) hangs from the midpoint of a cable whose two halves each make angle \( \theta \) with the horizontal. Derive the tension in the cable, and use your result to explain why the cable can never be pulled perfectly straight while it supports the load.
rubric: Knot/midpoint in equilibrium: horizontal components cancel by symmetry
Vertical: 2T sin θ = mg, so T = mg/(2 sin θ)
As θ → 0, sin θ → 0 and T → ∞
A horizontal cable has no vertical component, so it cannot balance the weight; any finite tension requires θ > 0 (a sag)
questions.why: Large tensions at shallow angles are the reason cables and their anchors must be far stronger than the loads they carry.

sections.title: Equilibrium in two dimensions

sections.md:
When the acceleration is not zero the procedure is the same, with \( ma_x \) and \( ma_y \) on the right-hand side. This section treats two standard situations: a body in an accelerating elevator, and several bodies joined by ropes.

**Apparent weight.** A bathroom scale measures the force with which it pushes up on you, a normal force, not your weight. This reading is your **apparent weight**. In an elevator with vertical acceleration \( a \) (positive upward), the forces on you are \( N \) up and \( mg \) down, so
\[ N - mg = ma \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = m(g + a). \]
Only the acceleration matters, not the velocity. The scale reads more than \( mg \) when the elevator speeds up going up or slows down going down (both have \( a > 0 \)); it reads less when the elevator speeds up going down or slows down going up; it reads exactly \( mg \) at constant velocity, moving or not. In free fall, \( a = -g \) and \( N = 0 \): the condition called weightlessness is zero apparent weight, not zero weight.

*Worked example.* A 70.0 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator; her weight is 686 N. Moving up and speeding up at 1.50 m/s²: \( N = 70.0(9.80 + 1.50) = 791 \) N. Moving up and slowing down at 1.50 m/s², so \( a = -1.50 \) m/s²: \( N = 70.0(8.30) = 581 \) N.

**Connected bodies.** Bodies joined by an ideal rope that stays taut move with equal speeds along the rope, so their accelerations have equal magnitudes. This **constraint** supplies the equation that the forces alone do not. Draw a separate free-body diagram for each body, choose each body's positive direction so that all move "forward" together, write the second law for each, and solve the equations simultaneously.

*Worked example (Atwood machine).* Masses \( m_1 = 2.00 \) kg and \( m_2 = 3.00 \) kg hang on either side of an ideal pulley from an ideal rope and are released from rest. The heavier mass descends. Take up as positive for \( m_1 \) and down as positive for \( m_2 \); by the constraint both have the same acceleration \( a \):
\[ m_1:\ T - m_1 g = m_1 a, \qquad m_2:\ m_2 g - T = m_2 a. \]
Adding the equations eliminates \( T \):
\[ a = \frac{(m_2 - m_1)g}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{(1.00)(9.80)}{5.00} = 1.96\ \text{m/s}^2, \qquad T = m_1(g + a) = \frac{2m_1m_2\,g}{m_1 + m_2} = 23.5\ \text{N}. \]
Check the result against limiting cases, a habit worth forming. For \( m_1 = m_2 \): \( a = 0 \) and \( T = mg \), equilibrium. For \( m_1 \to 0 \): \( a \to g \) and \( T \to 0 \), free fall. The tension, 23.5 N, lies between the two weights, 19.6 N and 29.4 N, as it must for one mass to accelerate upward and the other downward.

In the plot, the curve is the acceleration of \( m_2 \) (in m/s², downward positive) against \( m_2 \) (in kg). Drag the slider \( k \), the value of \( m_1 \) in kg. The acceleration is zero where \( m_2 = m_1 \) and approaches \( g \) (the horizontal line) as \( m_2 \) grows, without reaching it.

```plot
x: 0, 20
y: -10, 11
xlabel: m₂ (kg)
ylabel: a (m/s²)
slider: k, 0.5, 5, 2 | m₁ (kg)
f: 9.8*(x - k)/(x + k) | acceleration of m₂
hline: 9.8 | g
```

**Common mistakes.** Setting \( T = m_2 g \) for the descending mass: if the tension equaled its weight, the net force on it would be zero and it could not accelerate. Using one set of axes for both bodies and then writing the same symbol \( a \) for both accelerations; with common axes the constraint reads \( a_{1y} = -a_{2y} \), and it must be written explicitly.

questions.prompt: A 60.0 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is moving downward and speeding up at 2.20 m/s². Using \( g = 9.80 \) m/s², what does the scale read, in newtons?
questions.why: Moving down and speeding up means the acceleration is downward: \( a = -2.20 \) m/s² with up positive. \( N = m(g + a) = 60.0(9.80 - 2.20) = 456 \) N, less than her weight of 588 N.

questions.prompt: A block of mass \( m_1 \) (type `m1`) on a frictionless horizontal table is tied by an ideal rope, running over an ideal pulley at the table's edge, to a block of mass \( m_2 \) (type `m2`) hanging vertically. Give the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks in terms of \( m_1 \), \( m_2 \) and \( g \).
questions.why: Table block (toward the pulley positive): \( T = m_1 a \). Hanging block (down positive): \( m_2 g - T = m_2 a \). Adding: \( m_2 g = (m_1 + m_2)a \), so \( a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} \). Checks: \( m_1 \to 0 \) gives free fall; \( m_2 \to 0 \) gives \( a \to 0 \).

questions.model: The scale reads the normal force \( N \) on the passenger. With up positive, \( N - mg = ma \), so \( N = m(g + a) \). The reading depends only on the acceleration. An elevator moving downward can have an upward acceleration: this is the case when it is slowing down (for example, arriving at a lower floor). Then \( a > 0 \) and \( N > mg \), so yes, the reading exceeds her weight. While it moves down at constant speed, \( a = 0 \) and \( N = mg \). While it moves down and speeds up (leaving an upper floor), \( a < 0 \) and \( N < mg \).
questions.prompt: An elevator is moving downward. Can the scale reading of a passenger be greater than her weight? Justify with the second law, and describe the motion that produces each of the three cases (reading greater than, equal to, and less than her weight).
rubric: Scale reads N, with N − mg = ma (up positive), so N = m(g + a)
The reading depends on the acceleration, not on the direction of the velocity
Yes: moving down while slowing down means a > 0, so N > mg
Equal at constant velocity (a = 0); less when moving down and speeding up (a < 0)
questions.why: Velocity and acceleration are independent: the second law involves only the latter.

terms.d: A push or pull on a body by another body, by contact or at a distance; a vector measured in newtons.
The vector sum of all external forces on a body or system; it determines the acceleration through the second law.
A force on a chosen system exerted by something outside it; internal forces (between parts of the system) cancel in pairs.
